explanation.body:
Einstein's photoelectric equation with the stopping potential: $hf = \Phi + eV_s$.

$3.5\times10^{-19} = \Phi + (1.6\times10^{-19})(0.25)$, so $\Phi = 3.1\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}$.

perOption.A: Subtracts 0.25 eV twice (or adds wrongly); not the work function.
perOption.C: Ignores the stopping potential and takes the photon energy as the work function.
perOption.D: Adds $eV_s$ to the photon energy instead of subtracting it.

difficultyReason: One-step use of the photoelectric equation, with the stopping potential converted to joules.
misconception: Taking the photon energy as the work function

explanation.body:
Total binding energy before: $7.59\times235 = 1783.65\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

Total binding energy after: $(8.26\times121)+(8.52\times113) = 1962\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

Change in binding energy $= +179\ \mathrm{MeV}$, released as energy since the products are more stable. (The neutrons have no binding energy.)

perOption.A: Counts only part of the nucleons, or omits a product; gives 73.9 MeV.
perOption.B: Wrong magnitude and the wrong sense (absorbed).
perOption.C: Correct. Binding energy increases, so energy is released.
perOption.D: Right magnitude but the wrong sense; higher binding energy means energy is released.

difficultyReason: Needs total binding energy (per nucleon times nucleon number) and the sign convention for released versus absorbed.
misconception: Confusing binding energy increase with energy absorbed
transcription: Nuclear reaction: $^{235}_{92}\mathrm{U} + {}^1_0\mathrm{n} \to {}^{121}_{45}\mathrm{Rh} + {}^{113}_{47}\mathrm{Ag} + 2\,{}^1_0\mathrm{n}$. Binding energy per nucleon: U-235 = 7.59 MeV, Rh-121 = 8.26 MeV, Ag-113 = 8.52 MeV. What is the energy change in this reaction? A 73.9 MeV released. B 73.9 MeV absorbed. C 179 MeV released. D 179 MeV absorbed.

explanation.body:
$v = s/t = (385-115)/(3.50-1.50) = 270/2.00 = 135\ \mathrm{mm\,s^{-1}}$.

Add fractional uncertainties: $\dfrac{\Delta v}{v} = \dfrac{\Delta s}{s}+\dfrac{\Delta t}{t} = \dfrac{1+1}{270}+\dfrac{0.02+0.02}{2.00}$.

$\Delta v = 3.7 \approx 4\ \mathrm{mm\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Uses the uncertainty in time only and mishandles the ratio.
perOption.B: Combines the uncertainties incorrectly and gets a far too small value.
perOption.C: Uses a single reading uncertainty and ignores that differences add uncertainties.
perOption.D: Correct. Uncertainties in a difference add, then fractional uncertainties add for the quotient.

difficultyReason: Requires adding absolute uncertainties for each difference before adding fractional uncertainties.
misconception: Using a single reading uncertainty instead of the sum for a difference

explanation.body:
The second displacement is resultant minus first. Resolving gives a right-angled triangle with sides 150 cm and 140 cm.

Magnitude $=\sqrt{150^2+140^2} = 205\ \mathrm{cm}$.

Direction $= 90 - 30 - \tan^{-1}(140/150) = 17^\circ$ below the $x$-axis, i.e. $343^\circ$ anticlockwise from $+x$.

perOption.A: Adds magnitudes (150+140) and ignores the angles.
perOption.B: Adds magnitudes (150+140) and ignores the angles.
perOption.C: Correct magnitude but the angle is taken above the x-axis instead of below.

difficultyReason: Vector subtraction in two dimensions with an angle convention to interpret.
misconception: Taking the angle above rather than below the axis
transcription: A man pushing a mop makes two displacements. The first is 150 cm at $120^\circ$ anticlockwise from the positive $x$-axis [diagram shows the vector in the second quadrant]. The resultant is 140 cm at $30^\circ$ anticlockwise from $+x$. What are the magnitude and direction (anticlockwise from $+x$) of the second displacement? A 290 cm, $90^\circ$. B 290 cm, $270^\circ$. C 205 cm, $17^\circ$. D 205 cm, $343^\circ$.

explanation.body:
At the start: $1.2\times10^5 = 2(1.0\times10^5)a$, so $a = 0.60\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. At $t=20\ \mathrm{s}$, $v = 0.60\times20 = 12\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

The back carriage then moves at constant $12\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$: in 20 s it travels $240\ \mathrm{m}$.

The front carriage now has $a = 1.2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$: $s = 12(20)+\tfrac12(1.2)(20)^2 = 480\ \mathrm{m}$.

Separation $= 480-240 = 240\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Not obtained from the correct motion of either carriage.
perOption.B: Correct. Front 480 m minus back 240 m.
perOption.C: Not obtained from the correct motion of either carriage.
perOption.D: This is the distance travelled by the front carriage alone, not the separation.

difficultyReason: Chained kinematics: the front carriage's acceleration changes after the coupling breaks.
misconception: Forgetting that the front carriage's acceleration doubles once the rear one is shed

explanation.body:
Ball A: $h=\tfrac12 gt^2$ gives $t=\sqrt{2h/g}$, so $x_A = 2v\sqrt{2h/g}$.

Ball B: $2h=\tfrac12 gt^2$ gives $t=\sqrt2\sqrt{2h/g}$, so $x_B = v\sqrt2\sqrt{2h/g}$.

$\dfrac{x_A}{x_B} = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt2} = \sqrt2 = 1.41$.

perOption.A: Uses the speed ratio only and ignores the longer fall time of B (2.83 = $2\sqrt2$).
perOption.B: Correct. Time ratio is $1/\sqrt2$, speed ratio is 2.
perOption.C: Assumes the two effects cancel exactly.
perOption.D: Inverts the ratio or mishandles the time dependence (0.353).

difficultyReason: Needs time of fall $\propto\sqrt h$ combined with speed ratio.
misconception: Forgetting that fall time depends on height

explanation.body:
Whole system: $F-6f = 6Ma$, so $a = \dfrac{F-6f}{6M}$ (friction is proportional to mass: $f$, $2f$, $3f$).

For block $3M$: $F_1 - 3f = 3Ma$, so $F_1 = 3M\left(\dfrac{F-6f}{6M}\right)+3f = \dfrac F2$.

perOption.B: Adds $3f$ to $F/2$ again; friction on $3M$ is already included.
perOption.C: Splits $F$ equally between the three blocks.
perOption.D: Splits $F$ equally between the three blocks and adds friction wrongly.

difficultyReason: Apply Newton's second law to the system, then to a single block, with friction proportional to mass.
misconception: Ignoring that friction scales with each block's mass
transcription: Three blocks of masses $M$, $2M$, $3M$ (in that order, $M$ at the left) are pushed along a rough surface by a horizontal force $F$ applied to $M$. Friction on mass $M$ is $f$ and $f$ is proportional to $M$. What is the magnitude of the force that $3M$ exerts on $2M$? A $F/2$. B $F/2+3f$. C $F/3+f$. D $F/3+3f$.

explanation.body:
Conservation of momentum in the collision: $(5.0)(200) = (5.0+95)u$, so $u = 10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

Conservation of energy afterwards: $\tfrac12(100)(10^2) = (100)(9.81)H$, so $H = 5.1\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.B: Uses $g=10$ with $u$ wrongly, or ignores the combined mass.
perOption.C: Uses the pellet's speed or mass inconsistently.
perOption.D: Applies energy conservation to the pellet's initial speed (about 2000 m).

difficultyReason: Momentum conservation in a perfectly inelastic collision followed by energy conservation.
misconception: Applying energy conservation across the collision

explanation.body: The rack is in equilibrium under three forces (weight, the push from the bottle's neck at the top, and the table's contact force at the bottom). For three non-parallel forces in equilibrium, the lines of action must meet at a single point. Only diagram C satisfies this.

perOption.A: The lines of action do not meet at a point.
perOption.B: Forces are all vertical, so the torque cannot balance with the top force.
perOption.C: Correct. The three lines of action are concurrent.
perOption.D: The lines of action do not meet at a point.

difficultyReason: Needs the three-force concurrency rule applied to unfamiliar diagrams.
misconception: Treating the table reaction as purely vertical
transcription: [Diagram of a wine rack with a bottle balanced on a table; the rack is not attached to the base.] Which diagram (A to D) correctly shows the directions of the forces on the wine rack? [Four free-body diagrams of the slanted rack, with arrows at the top and bottom contact points and a downward weight at the centre.]

explanation.body:
For each mass, tension + upthrust = weight, so tension = weight $-$ upthrust.

The rod is horizontal and pivoted at its centre, so the tensions are equal.

Upthrust $=V\rho g$ is greater for P because liquid X is denser, so P's weight must be greater to give the same tension as Q.

perOption.A: Same volume but different liquid densities give different upthrusts.
perOption.B: P is in the denser liquid so its upthrust is larger, not smaller.
perOption.C: Reverses the conclusion: P needs the larger weight.
perOption.D: Correct. Larger upthrust on P means P must be heavier.

difficultyReason: Requires combining moment balance with upthrust.
misconception: Thinking equal moments imply equal weights
transcription: Two objects P and Q of the same volume hang from the ends of a light uniform rod pivoted at its centre; P is submerged in liquid X and Q in liquid Y. Density of X is greater than that of Y, and the system balances. Which statement is correct? A P and Q experience the same upthrust. B Upthrust on P is smaller than on Q. C Mass of P is smaller than mass of Q. D Mass of P is greater than mass of Q.

explanation.body:
Vertical: $T\cos30^\circ = mg$ (1). Horizontal: $T\sin30^\circ = mr\omega^2$ (2).

(2)/(1): $\tan30^\circ = r\omega^2/g$, with $r = 3.0+5.0\sin30^\circ = 5.5\ \mathrm{m}$.

$\omega = 1.01\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$, so $T = 2\pi/\omega = 6.2\ \mathrm{s}$.

perOption.A: Not from the correct radius or angular speed.
perOption.C: Uses $r=5.0\ \mathrm{m}$ or a wrong radius (omits the 3.0 m offset).
perOption.D: Correct. Radius of the circle is $3.0+5.0\sin30^\circ$.

difficultyReason: Radius includes an offset from the axle and the resolved tension supplies the centripetal force.
misconception: Using the string length as the circle radius
transcription: A mass $m$ on an inextensible string of length 5.0 m moves in a horizontal circle as a central axle rotates. The string is attached 3.0 m from the axle and makes $30^\circ$ with the vertical. What is the period of the motion about the axle? A 1.0 s. B 3.5 s. C 4.8 s. D 6.2 s.

explanation.body:
Tangentially: $F - mg\sin\theta = 0$. Radially: $T - mg\cos\theta = mr\omega^2$.

So $T = mr\omega^2 + mg\cos\theta$, which varies with $\cos\theta$.

Tension is largest at the lowest point ($\theta=0$) and smallest at the highest point ($\theta=\pi$), matching graph C.

perOption.A: Constant tension would need no weight component.
perOption.B: Has two cycles per revolution; $\cos\theta$ has one.

difficultyReason: Choose the right graph shape from $T = mr\omega^2 + mg\cos\theta$.
misconception: Thinking the tension is constant because the speed is constant
transcription: An object fixed to one end of a light rod rotates in a vertical circle at constant speed; $\theta$ is the angle of the rod from the downward vertical. Which graph could represent $T$ against $\theta$ from 0 to $2\pi$? [A: constant. B: two full oscillations, maximum at 0, $\pi$ and $2\pi$. C: cosine-like with a maximum at 0 and $2\pi$ and a minimum at $\pi$. D: starts low, maximum at $\pi$, falls to low at $2\pi$.]

explanation.body:
At P: $\Phi_P = -\dfrac{GM}{r/3}-\dfrac{GM_B}{2r/3} = -\dfrac Gr(3M+1.5M_B)$.

At Q: $\Phi_Q = -\dfrac{GM}{2r/3}-\dfrac{GM_B}{r/3} = -\dfrac Gr(1.5M+3M_B)$.

$\Phi_Q = 1.25\Phi_P$ gives $1.5M+3M_B = 1.25(3M+1.5M_B)$, so $M_B = 2M$.

perOption.A: Algebra slip in the potential contributions.
perOption.B: Uses the wrong distances for one planet.
perOption.C: Uses the wrong distances for one planet.
perOption.D: Correct. Add the potentials from both planets at each point.

difficultyReason: Superposition of potentials at two points, with algebra to solve for the unknown mass.
misconception: Using the wrong distance from each planet
transcription: Planet A (mass $M$) and planet B (unknown mass) have centres a distance $r$ apart. Points P and Q lie on the line joining them, dividing it into three equal parts of $r/3$ (P nearer A, Q nearer B). A spacecraft moving from P to Q has gravitational potential energy changing from $U$ to $1.25U$. What is the mass of B in terms of $M$? A $5M/4$. B $4M/3$. C $3M/2$. D $2M$.

explanation.body:
Gravitational force provides the centripetal force: $\dfrac{GMm}{r^2}=mr\omega^2$, so $\omega^2\propto 1/r^3$. When $r$ decreases, both the gravitational force and $\omega$ increase, so A and B are wrong.

$KE=+\dfrac{GMm}{2r}$ and $GPE=-\dfrac{GMm}{r}$. As $r$ decreases, KE increases while GPE decreases, so only D is correct.

difficultyReason: Standard qualitative results for circular orbits.
misconception: Thinking energy decreases in every form as the satellite moves closer

explanation.body:
Let $h$ be the rate of heat loss. Then $10 = \dfrac{mc\Delta\theta}{t}+h$ (1) and $18 = \dfrac{3mc\Delta\theta}{t}+h$ (2).

Subtracting: $8 = 2\dfrac{mc\Delta\theta}{t}$, so $\dfrac{mc\Delta\theta}{t}=4\ \mathrm{W}$, giving $h = 6.0\ \mathrm{W}$.

difficultyReason: Set up two simultaneous energy balance equations including heat loss.
misconception: Ignoring heat loss or assuming it changes with power
